source.title: Locality defeats the curse of dimensionality in convolutional teacher–student scenarios
source.authors: Alessandro Favero; Francesco Cagnetta; M. Wyart

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text contains the full paper and supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports kernel regression learning curves for local and convolutional kernels across filter sizes, data dimensions, and synthetic and CIFAR-10 settings. These results conceptually test whether locality and architecture affect generalization, but do not test the claim's random-label memorization, ordinary finite neural network training, or the specified architecture comparison.
record.gate_note: Results about learning-curve exponents, local versus convolutional students, and CIFAR-10 filter sizes bear on V3. The paper does not report comparisons of fully connected networks trained from scratch against convolutional networks, nor results for V1, V2, V4–V8. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows. Figure-only learning curves without a textual value are recorded as figure-only, not numerically reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study investigates locality and weight sharing through kernel-regression mean-squared-error learning curves. It does not measure V3's test-error comparison between convolutional and fully connected image classifiers trained from scratch with standard gradient methods. Its kernels and NTK experiments provide related mechanistic evidence, but do not test any stated version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct for representable targets: locality controls the learning exponent, while weight sharing changes sample requirements by a patch-count factor. The exponent is optimal at s = t; s < t prevents vanishing error. Ridgeless predictions use a heuristic spectral argument, and the decreasing-ridge result requires a Gaussian universality assumption.
record.recipe_differences: Teacher-student kernel regression with ridgeless or decreasing-ridge estimators; synthetic Gaussian-field targets and a CIFAR-10 binary-task kernel-regression experiment, rather than finite networks trained on natural labels with standard gradient methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Student filter size, teacher filter size, embedding dimension, local versus convolutional kernel, patch-count rescaling, and synthetic versus CIFAR-10 data affect the reported learning curves.

fits_no_version.finding: For representable synthetic convolutional targets with Laplacian constituents, local and convolutional students have learning exponent β = 1/s, independent of embedding dimension; full-input filters recover dimension-dependent rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Locality can improve the sample-scaling exponent of kernel-regression mean squared error on compositional targets.

fits_no_version.finding: Students with s < t cannot reproduce the target, and convolutional students cannot learn the tested local non-shift-invariant target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Kernel locality and invariance priors must allow representation of the target for error to vanish with more samples.

fits_no_version.finding: Local and convolutional learning curves overlap after plotting local-student sample size divided by the patch count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight sharing reduces sample requirements by a patch-count factor in the tested convolutional teacher-student setting without changing the asymptotic exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: CIFAR-10 regression exponents decrease as filter size rises: 0.19, 0.18, 0.17 for airplane/car and 0.11, 0.09, 0.07 for cat/dog.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Smaller local-kernel filters yield faster decay of held-out mean squared error on these two CIFAR-10 tasks.

record.problems: Evidence mainly concerns kernel regression on generated teacher-student targets rather than finite networks trained on natural labels. The CIFAR-10 experiment is a two-class kernel-regression task; its exponents are interpolated in the last decade, and no uncertainty values are stated there. The paper identifies its decreasing-ridge proof as relying on a Gaussian universality assumption.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible reported results were omitted. Learning-curve curves in Figure S3 and Figures S4–S5 are not separately rowed because the supplied text describes their analogous settings without giving separate textual numerical results; their specific plotted values are figure-only.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error when widening trained networks beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier test error under standard gradient training; learned sparse local connections; initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance and tuning conditions.
Batch-size penalties under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix G.2 says the CIFAR-10 exponent increases with filter size, contradicting Figure S6's numerical values and Section 5's smaller-filter conclusion. The record's fits_no_version entry repeats that apparent textual error. An untested classifier comparison does not warrant a limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label performance.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
The specified fully connected versus convolutional classifier comparison, and tests of learned sparse local connections or convolutional initialization.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with train-test gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: synthetic convolutional teacher with student filter size s ≥ t
reader_labels.reason: Local and convolutional kernels show learning curves governed by filter size, but the study does not test the specified classifier comparison (R1–R4, R7–R8). When s < t, errors do not decrease with more samples (R5–R6). On CIFAR-10, the reported exponent decreases as local filter size increases in both tasks (R10–R11).
